nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Shallow, clear water lets light reach the seagrass beds, and the arid land above gets strong sun year round.

nodes.name: Hypersaline water
nodes.desc: Hamelin Pool is about twice as salty as normal seawater, which suits stromatolite builders and keeps out animals that would graze them.

nodes.name: Warm, shallow, sheltered bay
nodes.desc: The bay is shallow, about 9 m deep on average, and its sheltered sandy floors carry some of the largest seagrass meadows known.

nodes.name: Red sand and limestone country
nodes.desc: Arid sandy land of the peninsulas and islands, home to the shrubs, grasses and ground-dwelling animals of the terrestrial side.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, stromatolite mats, carcasses and leaf litter, returning nutrients to the sediment and soil.

nodes.name: Ribbonweed
nodes.desc: A seagrass whose meadows in Shark Bay include one giant clone covering about 200 square km. Rhizomes anchor the sand and the leaves slow silt.

nodes.name: Wire weed
nodes.desc: A seagrass of southern and western Australian coasts that forms extensive meadows in shallow water on sand, gravel and rock.

nodes.name: Paddle weed
nodes.desc: A small, fast-growing seagrass that quickly colonises bare patches. Halophila is among the seagrasses dugongs eat most.

nodes.name: Stromatolite-building cyanobacteria
nodes.desc: Microbial mats at Hamelin Pool that trap sediment and cement it with calcium carbonate, building living stromatolites, the most diverse and abundant in the world.

nodes.name: Dune wattle
nodes.desc: A common scrub of coastal dunes and sandplains. Banded hare-wallabies favour thickets of it for shelter, and its seeds and foliage feed other animals.

nodes.name: Spear grasses
nodes.desc: Tussock grasses of the sandy mainland and island country, grazed and seeded on by ground-dwelling mammals.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: Shark Bay holds roughly 10,000 dugongs. They eat mainly seagrass, especially Halophila and Halodule, and their feeding opens space for fast-growing species to recolonise.

nodes.name: Green turtle
nodes.desc: Adults are mostly herbivorous, grazing seagrass and algae in shallow bays. Green turtles nest on sandy beaches in Shark Bay.

nodes.name: Western king prawn
nodes.desc: Bottom-dwelling prawn of sandy seabeds that makes up much of the catch of the Shark Bay prawn fishery. A food item for many fish.

nodes.name: Banded hare-wallaby
nodes.desc: A nocturnal vegetarian that shelters in dense thickets, favouring dune wattle scrub. Natural populations survive only on Bernier and Dorre islands; reintroduced to Dirk Hartog Island.

nodes.name: Boodie
nodes.desc: Burrowing bettong that eats seeds, roots, fungi, grasses and more. Its digging turns over soil and spreads seeds and fungi.

nodes.name: Whitings
nodes.desc: Small bottom-feeding fish of shallow sandy bays that eat small crustaceans and worms. Prey for dolphins, cormorants and sharks.

nodes.name: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: Eats a wide range of fish and squid. Some Shark Bay dolphins wear marine sponges on their snouts, seemingly as tools to probe the seabed for fish.

nodes.name: Pied cormorant
nodes.desc: A diving seabird that eats mostly small bottom-dwelling fish, with some prawns and other crustaceans.

nodes.name: Pacific gull
nodes.desc: A big gull that eats fish, crabs, cephalopods and other seashore animals, and scavenges scraps. Drops shellfish onto rocks to break them.

nodes.name: Sand goanna
nodes.desc: A relentless forager on mice, small mammals, birds, lizards and eggs. Adults also eat carrion.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: Has the widest diet of any shark, including fish, sea turtles, dugongs and dolphins. Dugongs shift feeding areas when sharks are abundant.

nodes.name: Feral cat
nodes.desc: Introduced predator ranked among the biggest threats to Australian mammals. Removed from Dirk Hartog Island so lost mammals could return.
